claims.text: Replacing EAM references with a machine-learning interatomic potential trained on ab initio solid and liquid configurations will improve reference–target phase-space overlap near alloy melting temperatures.
Improved phase-space overlap from the machine-learning reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The relevant multicomponent high-entropy alloys are typically equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The intervention is intended for alloys containing four or more principal elements.
The applicable temperature interval is approximately 0.8Tm to 1.2Tm.
Successful application requires the training data to cover the relevant configurational space.
A suitably trained machine-learning potential can accurately capture the many-body interactions and diverse configurations found in both solid and liquid states.
Training on a comprehensive set of ab initio configurations allows a machine-learning potential to reproduce the target potential-energy surface more faithfully.
More faithful reproduction of the potential-energy surface increases reference–target phase-space overlap.
Greater reference–target phase-space overlap reduces errors associated with the thermodynamic-integration path.
The fixed functional form of EAM is less able than the proposed machine-learning potential to represent the relevant solid and liquid configurations.
The machine-learning reference will produce less thermodynamic-integration path mismatch than TOR-TILD's EAM references.
Free-energy errors are expected to decrease by at least 20 percent.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the quality, diversity, and comprehensiveness of the training data.
The intervention is expected to be effective near the melting point when configurational sampling is sufficient.
The intervention may perform poorly for alloys with very asymmetric compositions.
The intervention may perform poorly outside its calibrated high-temperature range.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies an expected free-energy-error reduction of at least 20%, whereas the falsification rule uses an ambiguous 10–20% path-mismatch threshold. These are different quantities and do not define one consistent quantitative success criterion.
